source: Ross & Lo (2026) One Size Fits None: Heuristic Collapse in LLM Investment Advice
finding: Frontier LLMs acting as financial advisors lean on one or two inputs, mostly self-reported risk tolerance, and ignore the rest of the client profile. The authors call this heuristic collapse. In effect the models act like a one-reason rule.
numbers: 1,000 synthetic client profiles (Latin hypercube). Surrogate models fit to LLM allocations. Risk tolerance carried 57-88% of predictive weight in most models. GPT-4o without web search: equities feature concentration FC=0.780 (surrogate R2=0.882), tax-advantaged accounts FC=0.704 (R2=0.843), cash and savings FC=0.683 (R2=0.827). The GPT-5.4 family showed less collapse.
quote: the reduction of a complex, multi-factor decision to dependence on a small number of salient features
limits: Preprint. No ground truth for the right allocation, so it measures input sensitivity, not accuracy. Surrogate fit (R2) is the check on FC. Only investment advice. A one-reason rule can be fine in some environments; the paper judges it against a legal standard of individualised advice.
agent_relevance: A model can quietly act as take-the-best on a multi-cue task and still sound integrated. If our agent must weigh many cues, audit which cue the output tracks with a code-side sensitivity test, and do not trust the written rationale. Supports G5 (code selects).

source: Ross & Lo (2026) One Size Fits None: Heuristic Collapse in LLM Investment Advice (mitigation results)
finding: Web search only partly reduced the collapse, and unevenly. Whether the tool was used at all depended on how it was asked for.
numbers: GPT-4o with web search, change in feature concentration: cash and savings -65%, tax-advantaged accounts -45%, equities +16%, fixed income near zero. GPT-5.4 Mini and Nano showed small increases for equities. Web search used in 0% of profiles when merely available, 0.7% when encouraged, 99.9% when required. Round numbers: 89-100% of allocations were multiples of 5 without search (GPT-4o 100%).
limits: Single domain, a handful of models, preprint. Surrogate-based measure. The round-number habit is a second cheap heuristic that no prompt asked for.
agent_relevance: Adding information (search, more context) does not by itself widen the cues a model uses. A tool must be forced by code (required, not offered) to change behaviour. Matches our rule that the program, not the model, decides what happens next.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free Energy Heuristics: Fast-and-Frugal Cognition as Active Inference Under Uncertain Precision
finding: Theory paper. Under uncertainty about how precise one's own evidence is, the policy that minimises expected free energy stops after a few top cues. Under a stated condition (Descending Dominance, cues ordered by validity) that policy gives the same choice as take-the-best on every cue pattern. With equal cue validity it matches tallying. It predicts that longer chain-of-thought hurts on questions with no determinate answer.
numbers: Take-the-best equivalence checked numerically: 26,696 sample-wise comparisons under 200 random profiles satisfying the condition, 0 mismatches. Tallying equivalence under uniform validity checked over 30 permutations, 0 violations. Recognition heuristic, satisficing and fast-and-frugal trees are only conjectured.
quote: Fast-and-frugal heuristics and active inference are, in the meta-uncertain regime, two descriptions of the same computation.
limits: Single-author arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. Proofs depend on a Gaussian-Gamma model and the Descending Dominance condition. Mapping to real LLM internals is by behavioural proxy only.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal reason to cut deliberation when the question is open: a candidate rule for S0 (choose direct mode or abstain when the class has no determinate answer). It is a hypothesis; the next two lines are its empirical test.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free Energy Heuristics: Fast-and-Frugal Cognition as Active Inference Under Uncertain Precision (pre-registered LLM test)
finding: Pre-registered test: on unanswerable (Knightian) questions, telling the model to reason step by step lowered the rate of correctly saying 'this cannot be determined'. On matched questions with definite answers, reasoning length had almost no effect.
numbers: 7 models (phi3.5, mistral-7B, Qwen2.5 7B/14B/32B, claude-sonnet-4-5, gpt-4o), 45 items (31 high-uncertainty, 14 controls), 5 reasoning-length conditions, 5 replications = 7,875 responses. High-uncertainty accuracy by condition: direct 77.1%, then 66.5%, 64.7%, 64.4%, 62.1% for longer reasoning. Controls: 83.7% direct, short-to-long drop 1.73 points. Pooled raw drop 12.7 points; difference-in-differences 10.97. Hierarchical model: interaction beta3 = -0.692, posterior P(beta3<0)=1.0000, implied drop 17.3 points (95% credible interval 7.7 to 25.5). Qwen2.5-14B fell almost 40 points.
limits: Regime assigned by item category, not by the pre-registered continuous score (disclosed deviation). Scoring is abstention on unanswerable items, narrower than accuracy in general. Only 45 items. Effect strong in mid-to-large models, directional in the two frontier models, absent or reversed in the two weakest. Preprint, one author, not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a lean mode beats deliberation on open questions. Our S0 class record could carry a flag for 'no determinate answer / no base rate' and route that class to direct or abstain. Test on our own items first; the controls show it is not a general rule.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free Energy Heuristics: Fast-and-Frugal Cognition as Active Inference Under Uncertain Precision (scope and boundary)
finding: The paper limits its own claim: instructed reasoning hurts some models badly, barely touches others, and reverses in the weakest. Realised step count is endogenous, so the randomly assigned length condition is the primary contrast.
numbers: Controls show a small generic cost of long reasoning (beta1 = -0.183); the high-regime penalty is about four times larger. P(high-regime effect larger in size than low-regime effect) = 0.905. The regime score (cross-prompt variance, cross-seed variance, calibration error) was validated by simulate-and-recover (rho above 0.96).
limits: Not an independent replication. No test of take-the-best, recognition or tallying as prompts. The link from the maths to the behaviour is argued, not measured.
agent_relevance: Boundary note: mode choice by class must be validated per model size. A small model may not show the effect, so do not hard-code the rule from one model.

source: Zheng, Zhou & Wang (2025) Beyond Nash Equilibrium: Bounded Rationality of LLMs and humans in Strategic Decision-making
finding: In rock-paper-scissors and prisoner's dilemma, LLMs use the same simple human rules (outcome-based play such as win-stay, lose-change) but apply them more rigidly and in a more exaggerated form. Model families show distinct strategy signatures.
numbers: Outcome-dependent play (chi-square test): 36 of 90 human participants versus 63 of 126 model runs. Models include Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3/R1 and OpenAI o1 (from the reference list and text).
limits: Two small games. Only part of the paper was read (abstract, setup, outcome-dependence counts, discussion); garbled two-column text limited parsing. Not a test of the adaptive toolbox as such.
agent_relevance: Heuristic play in a model is rigid: it does not adapt the rule to the opponent as people do. If the agent uses a rule-of-thumb mode, code must monitor whether the rule still pays off (an environment-fit check), because the model will not.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee & Nguyen (2024) Do Large Language Models Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans? A Case Study Using GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 shows the classic Kahneman-Tversky effects that humans show: anchoring, conjunction fallacy, availability, framing, endowment. This is the heuristics-and-biases side, not the ecological-rationality side (a parallel subfield).
numbers: Anchoring: mean estimate low anchor 20.83 (ChatGPT) vs 22.50 (humans); high anchor 105.97 vs 80.50. Conjunction fallacy: ChatGPT chose the conjunction 18 of 20 times, humans 10 of 20. Endowment: ChatGPT kept the owned coin in 37 of 40 trials (92.5%), humans 34 of 40 (85%).
limits: Small samples (20 to 40 trials per cell), one old model, prompts with a role-play framing ('pretend you are an agent who can do anything'). Confidence intervals in the extracted text were hard to parse, so only counts and means are recorded.
agent_relevance: Shows the failure side: shortcuts in models are inherited from text, not chosen to fit the environment. Ecological rationality asks when a shortcut is good; here nothing selected it. A reason for code-side gating of any fast mode.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (published version: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT)
finding: On Cognitive Reflection Test items and semantic illusions, early GPT-3 models answered intuitively and wrongly, like people. ChatGPT and GPT-4 stopped doing so, mostly by writing out chain-of-thought.
numbers: CRT correct: 5% GPT-3 davinci-003, 59% ChatGPT-3.5, 96% GPT-4, 38% humans. Intuitive (trap) answers: 80% davinci-003, 15% ChatGPT-3.5, 0% GPT-4, 55% humans. Semantic illusions: davinci-003 fell for them 72% of the time; correct answers 18% davinci-003, 74% ChatGPT-3.5, 88% GPT-4. ChatGPT-3.5 used chain-of-thought in 97% of CRT answers, GPT-4 in 85%.
limits: Old models. 'Intuition' here means the wrong trap answer, not a useful heuristic. Human figures are a reference sample (CRT 41% in the original, n=3,428).
agent_relevance: A model's fast answer is only as good as the match between task and shortcut. The fix that worked here was written-out steps, but later studies (below) show that fix backfires on some task classes. Mode choice should therefore depend on class.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) - prompting and suppressing chain-of-thought (Studies 2-3)
finding: Adding a step-by-step prompt lifted GPT-3 davinci-003 on CRT. Suppressing chain-of-thought in ChatGPT-4 cost little, so a strong model keeps most accuracy with reasoning off on this item class.
numbers: Step-by-step prompting: correct 5% to 28%, trap answers 80% to 29%. Suppressing chain-of-thought: ChatGPT-3.5 correct unchanged (change 4%, p=.49); ChatGPT-4 correct 95% to 88%, trap answers 0% to 10%. With training examples: one task type went from 2% to 92% after two examples, another from 12% to 92% after seven, and one reached about 78% after 30 examples.
limits: CRT items are a narrow, well-known set. Training-example effects hold within the task type only.
agent_relevance: This is the kind of per-class evidence the S0 record needs: pass rate of direct versus longer modes for each item class.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 solved many decision tasks as well as or better than people and beat humans on a multi-armed bandit, but showed no directed exploration, failed causal reasoning, and small rewording of vignettes broke it.
numbers: On the three Cognitive Reflection Test items GPT-3 gave the intuitive wrong answer every time. Changing the option order in a Wason-style item, or a detail of a CRT item, led it astray. In the two-armed bandit it showed no directed exploration and no horizon-sensitive random exploration (no significant interaction with horizon).
limits: GPT-3 (2022), long superseded. Exact sample sizes not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Model heuristics are brittle to surface changes in wording. A toolbox rule is safe only if the class label comes from code that reads structure, not from the model's reading of surface features.

source: Jagadish, Binz, Saanum, Wang & Schulz (2025) Meta-learning ecological priors from large language models explains human learning and decision making (ERMI)
finding: Instead of hand-building each heuristic, the authors have an LLM (Claude-v2) generate thousands of tasks and meta-learn a small transformer on them. In paired-comparison decisions the resulting model uses the same type of rule people use in each condition: one-reason when cue ranking is known, equal weighting when only cue direction is known, a weighted sum when neither is known.
numbers: About 7,000 tasks per condition. Gini coefficient of attribute weights: ranking 0.3399 (SEM 0.0631), direction 0.0743 (SEM 0.0138), unknown 0.1794 (SEM 0.0333). Fit to human choices (posterior model frequency): 0.7299 with two attributes, 0.6284 with four. Function learning: about 10,000 tasks of 20 points; category learning about 10,000 tasks; checks on 60 real regression tasks and 28 OpenML-CC18 classification tasks.
limits: Needs an LLM to write plausible task distributions. Cognitive-model study, not an agent loop. Only the first 100k of 158k characters of the page, plus the local PDF text for the decision section, were read.
agent_relevance: Ecological rationality can be learned instead of hand-coded: the right rule family follows the structure of the environment. For our agent this supports building the class-to-mode map from measured per-class pass rates, which is already the plan.

source: Jagadish et al. (2025) ERMI - other tasks (function and category learning)
finding: The same LLM-generated priors reproduce human learning curves and difficulty orderings across 15 experiments, in most cases better than rule-based or exemplar baselines.
numbers: Shepard-type error probability 0.0201 (type 1) to 0.2048 (type 6). Little et al. 2024 function learning: interpolation MSE 0.0171 vs 0.0256 for meta-learning without ecological priors, extrapolation 0.0223 vs 0.0424. Badham et al. 2017 posterior model frequency: ERMI 0.43, RMC 0.41. Devraj et al. 2021: ERMI 0.32, GCM 0.24, Rule 0.20.
limits: Fit to human data, not agent task accuracy. Comparisons depend on the baselines chosen. Single group.
agent_relevance: Background only: the machine-side proof that environment statistics, not hand rules, can supply the fit. Not directly usable in our loop.

source: Jagadish et al. (2025) ERMI - generator model comparison (methods remarks)
finding: The quality of the ecological prior depends on the generator model. Llama-3.1 (70B) matched Claude-v2 on decision-making datasets; GPT-4 sampled features from a uniform distribution and wrote only simple rules; non-tuned Llama-2 could not follow the format.
numbers: Qualitative; no accuracy numbers given for the weaker generators.
limits: Methods-section remarks, not a controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: If a model ever writes task or rule distributions for us, validate the statistics in code (feature distribution, correlation structure) before use.

source: Simsek & Buckmann (2015) Learning from small samples: an analysis of simple decision heuristics (NIPS 2015)
finding: Simple pairwise-comparison heuristics (single cue, take-the-best, greedy lexicographic, tallying) learn fast from very few examples. With very small training sets tallying does best; with half the objects for training all are close to logistic regression.
numbers: 63 natural datasets. Trained on 50% of objects, mean accuracy: logistic regression 0.747, CART 0.746, greedy lexicographic and take-the-best 0.743, single cue 0.734, tallying 0.725. One training pair already gives at least 83% of the best reachable accuracy for a single-cue rule (analytic result). Single cue was 0.9 points behind take-the-best and 1.3 behind logistic regression. Highest standard error 0.0014.
limits: Old computational study, not an LLM. Pairwise comparison tasks, mostly small datasets, independent pairs.
agent_relevance: Gives the sample-size boundary for a toolbox: with very few examples (cold start of a new class record), a unit-weight rule is the safest. Our S0 class record could start as tallying of pass/fail evidence and move to richer estimates only after more items.

source: Phillips, Neth, Woike & Gaissmaier (2017) FFTrees: A toolbox to create, visualize, and evaluate fast-and-frugal decision trees
finding: An R package that builds fast-and-frugal trees (one cue per level, an exit at each level) from data. Across ten real datasets the trees predicted as well as standard algorithms while using about two cues.
numbers: Mean balanced accuracy on held-out data: SVM 0.86 (SVM crashed on two datasets), fast-and-frugal trees 0.83, regularised logistic regression 0.83, random forests 0.83. Mean cues used: fan algorithms 1.85, zig-zag 4.85, max 6.5. Balanced accuracy: fan algorithms 0.81, max 0.64, zig-zag 0.75. 100 simulations per dataset-model pair. Weakest relative result: occupancy dataset, trees 0.96.
limits: Ten datasets chosen by the authors, mostly small. Balanced accuracy only. Fan algorithms were slower to build (median 2.61 s and 15.93 s vs 0.59 s).
agent_relevance: A concrete machine-side pattern for S0: a short sequence of code-checked yes/no questions about the item, each with an exit, classifies nearly as well as a fitted model. Use as the shape of the class-to-mode router (few cues, early exit).

source: Martignon, Erickson & Viale (2022) Transparent, simple and robust fast-and-frugal trees and their construction
finding: Methods paper on building fast-and-frugal trees by hand or with the CODAP/Arbor tool, framed as machine-aided decisions a person can read and trust. Compares trees with naive Bayes, logistic regression and CART on many datasets.
numbers: Benchmark design: five classifiers, 1,000 random splits per classifier, training samples of 15%, 50% and 90% of each dataset. Worked example is the Green and Mehr (1997) coronary care tree (first node: elevated ST segment).
limits: Conceptual and tutorial; numeric result tables were not extracted. Robustness claims cite Luan et al. 2011, Woike et al. 2017 and Martignon and Laskey 2019 rather than new data. PDF text partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Supports the design choice that the router should be readable and auditable. A tree the program can print is easier to test and revise than a model's judgement.

source: Chen, Zaharia & Zou (2023) FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
finding: An LLM cascade asks cheap models first and stops as soon as a learned score says the answer is reliable. That is a sequential, stop-at-first-sufficient rule, the same shape as a fast-and-frugal tree, applied across models. It matched GPT-4 at far lower cost.
numbers: Abstract: matches the best single model with up to 98% cost reduction, or +4% accuracy at equal cost. HEADLINES case: accuracy 0.872 vs GPT-4 0.857, cost $6.5 vs $33.1 (about 80% cheaper, +1.5%). Learned rule: query GPT-J, stop if score at least 0.96; else J1-Large, stop if at least 0.37; else GPT-4. Cascade length 3. Datasets: HEADLINES, OVERRULING, COQA.
limits: Mid-2023 models and prices. 'Up to' is a best case. Needs labelled data to learn thresholds; the scoring function is itself a model. The link to fast-and-frugal trees is my reading, not claimed by the authors.
agent_relevance: A working LLM-loop precedent for 'stop when a cheap check is confident'. In our loop the stop signal should come from code (a held-out check passes) instead of a learned score, but the cost structure is the same.

source: Chen, Zaharia & Zou (2023) FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance - diversity result
finding: Cheap models are sometimes right where the expensive one is wrong, so a cascade can beat the top model. This is a less-is-more effect at system level.
numbers: On HEADLINES, about 6% of cases: GPT-4 wrong while GPT-J (or J1-Large or GPT-C) is right (maximum performance improvement metric).
limits: Complementarity measured on three datasets. Gains need a reliable scoring function; a bad one passes wrong cheap answers.
agent_relevance: Warns against assuming the strongest model is always the right first tool. It also supports G4: diverse attempts, not copies of one model, are what add value.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Across published results, chain-of-thought helps a lot on math, logic and symbolic tasks and little elsewhere. On MMLU nearly all the gain sits in questions with an equals sign.
numbers: Meta-analysis of 110 papers, 1,218 comparisons, 264 datasets. Gains: symbolic reasoning +14.2 points, math +12.3, logical reasoning +6.9. In those three categories the average is 56.9 with chain-of-thought vs 45.5 without; in all other categories 56.8 vs 56.1. Own runs: 20 datasets, 14 LLMs. Up to 95% of the chain-of-thought gain on MMLU comes from questions with an equals sign. About 32% (59) of knowledge, soft reasoning and commonsense datasets showed a significant gain.
limits: Read through a fetch of the first 100k of 161k characters. The equals-sign split is a proxy for maths. Conclusions hold for 2023-2024 models and prompts.
agent_relevance: Strong class-level evidence for the S0 idea: long reasoning pays only in some task classes. Direct or short mode as default for knowledge, commonsense and reading tasks; extended reasoning kept for math, symbolic and logic classes.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
finding: Chain-of-thought lowered accuracy on tasks where deliberation also hurts people: implicit statistical learning, face recognition, and learning classes with exceptions. It helped on logical inconsistency (NLI) for some models. The human-psychology link predicted where it hurts.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning, zero-shot vs chain-of-thought: GPT-4o 87.5% vs 64.4%, Claude 3 Opus 70.7% vs 62.7%, Llama 3.1 70B 65.9% vs 57.1%. Up to 36.3 points lower for o1-preview (57.7%) vs GPT-4o zero-shot (94.0% on a 440-problem subset). Face recognition: GPT-4o 64.0% vs 51.2%, Claude 3 Opus 44.0% vs 29.6%. Rounds to learn exceptions: GPT-4o 2.9 direct vs 12.5 with chain-of-thought; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2.3 vs 6.4. Three of six tasks showed significant drops; the other three were mixed. NLI: GPT-4o MNLI 53.2% to 93.9% with chain-of-thought.
limits: o1-preview always reasons, so its baseline is GPT-4o. Older models (mid-2024). Six tasks. The cup-tilting spatial task was flat (GPT-4o 38% vs 40%).
agent_relevance: Names three task classes where deliberate modes are suspect: patterns learned from many examples without a stated rule, perceptual matching, and rules with exceptions. Add these to the S0 class features and test direct versus long mode per class.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind Your Step - feature aggregation task (apartment choice)
finding: On picking the better option from several weighted features (a cue-integration task close to the take-the-best versus weighted-sum paradigm), chain-of-thought mostly helped the strong models, and one open model collapsed.
numbers: Accuracy zero-shot vs chain-of-thought by gap in true score. Claude 3.5 Sonnet: 50% vs 62% (gap 0.1-0.3), 62% vs 72% (0.3-0.5), 81% vs 95% (0.5-1). GPT-4o: 47% vs 45%, 57% vs 56%, 80% vs 87%. Claude 3 Opus: 35% vs 50%, 57% vs 58%, 72% vs 84%. Llama 3.1 70B: 42% vs 6%, 44% vs 5%, 43% vs 20%.
limits: A weighted-sum judgement is a case where the compensatory rule is the right tool; the paper does not test a lexicographic or tallying prompt. The Llama collapse may be a format failure; only accuracy is reported.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: when the environment is compensatory, fuller reasoning helps. Do not generalise 'less is more' beyond tasks whose structure favours it.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
finding: Giving reasoning models longer reasoning budgets lowered accuracy on several task families: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, and constraint-tracking deduction. Five distinct failure modes were identified, and they differ by model family.
numbers: Models: Claude Sonnet 3.7/4 and Opus 4, o3-mini/o4-mini/o3, Qwen3-32B, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek R1. Misleading Math (2,500 questions, controlled): Opus 4 from near 100% to about 85-90%. Natural setup: R1 from about 70% to about 30% with five distractors. Misleading Python: Opus 4 near-perfect to about 80%. Safety item 'survival instinct': Sonnet 4 safe answers about 60% to 47%; o3 72% to 76%. Zebra puzzles (200): all models degrade in the natural setup, R1 most. Grades regression: study hours correlate 0.73 with the true grade; Opus 4 shifted weight to sleep and stress zero-shot. Few-shot examples largely removed the regression effect.
limits: Several figures are read from plots and given only approximately. Read through a fetch of the first 100k of 214k characters. Task families are synthetic. Models differ, so it is not a single law.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1 (do not deliberate by default). The failure mode 'shift from sound priors to spurious cues' is the opposite of ecological rationality: more thought, worse cue choice. Few-shot examples counter it, which fits the idea that the environment (the examples) fixes the right cue.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend large token budgets on easy problems, with later solution rounds adding little. Self-training to prefer shorter reasoning cut tokens roughly in half with accuracy held.
numbers: o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on average. QwQ example for '2+3': 13 solutions, 901 tokens, first solution 39 tokens (4.3%). QwQ-32B-Preview after self-training (accuracy before to after; tokens before to after): ASDIV 96.9 to 96.8, 741.8 to 381.6 (-48.6%); GSM8K 94.8 to 96.0, 772.8 to 416.6 (-46.1%); MATH500 93.0 to 92.8, 2407.9 to 1330.7 (-44.7%); GPQA 59.6 to 59.1, 3228.4 to 2085.7 (-35.4%); AIME24 46.7 to 43.3, 9480.9 to 5154.5 (-45.6%).
limits: One base model for the training result. The paper's introduction quotes 48.6% for MATH500 but its table gives 44.7% (my calculation; 48.6% is the ASDIV row). AIME24 accuracy fell (46.7 to 43.3, tiny test set).
agent_relevance: Machine-side frugality result: the first solution round is usually enough on easy items. Supports a code-side stop rule (stop when the first check passes) and difficulty-based mode choice.

source: Nikankin, Reusch, Mueller & Belinkov (2025) Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
finding: Inside the model, arithmetic is done by a sparse set of neurons that each fire for a simple pattern (for example an operand in a range). The unordered combination explains most of the accuracy. The model carries a bag of heuristics, not a general algorithm.
numbers: Abstract page only; no percentages were available on the page I read.
limits: Abstract only. Mechanistic claims about specific models. 'Heuristic' here means a narrow learned feature, not a Gigerenzer-style rule chosen for an environment.
agent_relevance: Models hold many local shortcuts that are reliable only in the range seen in training. A class record should treat accuracy outside the seen range as unknown, which fits our held-out rule (G3).

source: Search log for this angle (arXiv API, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, web search, 2026-10-26)
finding: I found no study that prompts or tests an LLM with take-the-best, the recognition heuristic, tallying or fast-and-frugal trees as its target, and none that measures an LLM agent loop built on Gigerenzer's adaptive toolbox. Closest hits: Bogdan (2026, theory plus test) and the Jagadish group (2024, 2025, cognitive-model side).
numbers: Queries tried: 'take-the-best language model', 'fast-and-frugal language model', 'recognition heuristic language models', 'adaptive toolbox LLM', 'ecological rationality language model', 'fast-and-frugal tree LLM', 'LLM lexicographic compensatory', and variants. The arXiv API returned 0 hits for several exact phrases. Semantic Scholar was rate limited.
limits: Absence in these indexes, not proof. Work labelled 'bounded rationality' or 'heuristics' in LLM papers mostly means Kahneman-Tversky biases (Suri 2024), game play (Zheng 2025) or hand-designed search heuristics (LLM-A*, EoH), which are not this topic.
agent_relevance: The adaptive toolbox is untested as a prompt or scaffold for LLMs. Any gain for our agent has to come from our own per-class measurement. This is also an opening: a measured direct versus short versus checked mode comparison by item class would be new.
